summary:
swyx opens by declaring war on "slop," defining it as low-quality, inauthentic, or inaccurate content generated by either humans or AI—not exclusively AI-produced, contrary to the Oxford English Dictionary's definition. He positions slop's opposite as "kino" and illustrates that the same tools, studios, models, and startup ideas can produce either kino or slop depending on execution and timing. He traces AI Engineer summit history from recognizing AI engineering as a discipline, to leadership, to model labs, to expanding the TAM with AIPMs, designers, and code summits, with coding as this year's central theme.

He frames the fight against slop as an asymmetric war, invoking Brandolini's law and proposing his own "law of anti-slop": the taste needed to fight slop is an order of magnitude greater than that needed to produce it, because token generation costs are dropping 100–1000x annually. He catalogs real-world code slop consequences from the past year including tech debt and private data exposure, and critiques autonomy claims that cite hours of operation without assessing code quality, coining "no autonomy without accountability" alongside "no taxation without representation."

He presents multiple AI-powered defenses: using AI to curate news (AI News newsletter), explicitly prompting models to avoid slop, semi-sync workflows that preserve human attention for hard problems while async-ing commoditized work, AI-powered code maps for codebase understanding, computer use for autonomous app operation, and sub-agents to combat context rot. He references Greg Brockman's modularity principle—clear human-designed boundaries with AI filling in between. The talk closes with an interactive call-and-response chant of "No more slop" applied to demanding bosses, insufficiently tested releases, and engagement-bait algorithms.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Opening and Context
sections.summary: swyx opens nervously, declares war on slop, and traces the evolution of AI Engineer summits from recognizing AI engineering as a discipline through expanding to leadership, model labs, and broader TAM including AIPMs, designers, and code summits. He notes coding is this year's theme but asks for five minutes to discuss slop.

sections.title: Defining Slop and Kino
sections.summary: swyx references Oxford English Dictionary's slop definition, disputes that slop requires AI, and shows the opposite of slop is kino. He illustrates that the same studios, models, and startup ideas can produce kino or slop depending on execution and timing, with examples from Netflix productions, Sora videos, and vibe coding approaches.

sections.title: Asymmetric War and the Law of Anti-Slop
sections.summary: Invoking Brandolini's law, swyx proposes his own law of anti-slop: the taste needed to fight slop is an order of magnitude greater than that needed to produce it, driven by token costs dropping 100–1000x annually. He positions taste elevation as a fundamental human responsibility.

sections.title: AI-Powered Defenses Against Slop
sections.summary: swyx catalogs defenses: AI News newsletter curation, explicit anti-slop prompting, semi-sync workflows preserving human attention for hard problems, code maps for codebase understanding, computer use for autonomous app operation including Devon for website updates, and sub-agents to fight context rot. He references Greg Brockman's modularity principle.

sections.title: Code Slop and Accountability
sections.summary: He catalogs real-world code slop consequences from the year including tech debt and private data exposure of millions of users. He critiques autonomy claims citing 30–60 hours without code quality metrics, coining "no autonomy without accountability" paralleling "no taxation without representation."

sections.title: Closing Call and Response
sections.summary: swyx compresses his message to "No more slop" and leads the audience in interactive call-and-response applying the phrase to demanding bosses, insufficiently tested releases, and engagement-bait algorithms, then closes the keynote.
